title: CI Intermittent segmentation fault in Windows arm64 wheels test (vanilla CPython)
body:
It's been seen so far (October 13) in 2 runs over 13 runs (see [scheduled Wheels runs](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/actions/workflows/wheels.yml?query=event%3Aschedule)):
- Python 3.12 [build log](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/actions/runs/18239153780/job/51938405934)
- Python 3.14 see [build log](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/actions/runs/18423960080/job/52502560141) from https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/32393#issuecomment-3396312539

The information is similar in both cases seems to point the finger at
```
sklearn\tree\tests\test_monotonic_tree.py", line 511 in test_nd_tree_nodes_values
```

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: Note that this test relies on the `global_random_seed` fixture, and our nightly run will try different seed values between 0 and 99 each night. It's possible to run that test for all admissible seeds by setting the `SKLEARN_TESTS_GLOBAL_RANDOM_SEED` environment variable to the `"all"` value and then run `pytest -vlk test_nd_tree_nodes_values`.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: BTW, maybe we should run pytest with the `-v` flag to display the seed value in the test name before failure.

2. you use action-tmate to have an interactive session in the GHA runner (optional as well, if you know how to do 3. in a non-interactive way)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant1 asking an LLM it seems like you can use CDB on Windows, please double-check this information and also investigate if it's installed on Windows arm runner images ...

WinDbg / CDB from Windows Debugging Tools

Microsoft's WinDbg or CDB (command-line WinDbg) can achieve similar backtrace extraction, but with different commands.

To run a program and automatically break on crash capturing a backtrace:

```
cdb -c "g; kb; q" program.exe
```

- `g` runs the program
- `kb` shows the stack backtrace
- `q` quits after

So I guess if you can reproduce on the CI from time to time you could do (may not work on Linux you need `gdb --args` to pass additional arguments maybe there is a cdb equivalent):
```
cdb -c "g; kb: q" python -m pytest sklearn
```

and post the stack-trace once you manage to get the segmentation fault.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
There's one known issue with Cython and Windows ARM: if you have sufficiently large tuple or list constants (~40 elements or more) then you can end up with the first element(s?) being wrongly initialized.

This is ultimately [an MSVC compiler bug](https://<redacted-host>/t/CC-Bad-code-generation-with-large-n/10952684) and we just had to disable a couple of our tests because of it - I couldn't see a non-disruptive way to work around it.

I'm not convinced that this is your issue - we found it typically just gave the wrong elements in a container rather than a crash but I'm sure you could engineer a situation where it crashes if you tried hard enough. I mention it just because it is a known issue so it's something that might be worth looking for.

I think Numpy uses clang-cl rather than MSVC for their Windows+Arm wheels. It might something to try because I expect their code-generation might be better in general (unfortunately setuptools doesn't know how to handle it - I don't know if that's a problem for you or not)

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
@participant3 thanks for the insights!

Just to make sure I get the basics right, a few questions:
- is `PyInit__utils` related to module initialization through Cython?
- does that means the issue happens at import time?
- any idea what to look for in our pyx or pxd file that could lead to such a problem? Besides `cnp.import_array()` I don't see much code being run at import time, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/tree/_utils.pyx

Last question: I suppose you haven't heard of a Windows arm specific issue in the Cython issue tracker?

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Yes - `PyInit__utils` is the Cython module initialization. And yes it's run at import time. However it's *very* light-weight - it just returns an object that tells Python what functions to call to do the "real" initialization. So I'm fairly sure that even `cnp.import_array()` will be being run later in a different function. 

> I suppose you haven't heard of a Windows arm specific issue in the Cython issue tracker?

I know of one Windows ARM bug (to do with initialization of large tuples and lists). I suspect you're issue isn't this one, but that's a guess.

It could well be a threading issue of some sort - ARM is more sensitive that x86 to threading. Additionally, MSVC has to go through some weird non-standard atomic functions because they don't believe in following the C standard. So that's something to be suspicious of. Unfortunately things like "thread-sanitizer" (which I'd normally recommend for diagnosing this kind of bug) just don't work on MSVC.
